claims.text: In refractory BCC high-entropy alloys, unusually high strength is mainly governed by edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations also mainly govern the unusually high hardness of refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
Plastic flow in conventional BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys is generally controlled by screw dislocations.
Atomic-size mismatch in refractory HEAs creates lattice distortions that strongly hinder edge-dislocation motion.
Atomic-size mismatch increases the density and pinning of edge dislocations.
NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV are examples of refractory BCC HEAs whose strength is associated with edge dislocations.
The proposed initial alloys have significant lattice distortion and a high prevalence of edge dislocations.
The density and mobility of edge dislocations are strongly affected by local lattice distortions arising from compositional complexity.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion promotes the formation and effective pinning of edge dislocations.
Pinned edge dislocations raise the energy barrier for dislocation motion and thereby increase hardness and yield strength.
Alloys with greater lattice distortion will have a higher density of pinned edge dislocations than alloys with lower lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion will produce higher hardness and yield strength than lower lattice distortion.
Refractory BCC HEAs governed by edge dislocations will soften more slowly with increasing temperature than conventional screw-controlled BCC alloys.
A NbTaTiZrV0.5 HEA exhibits an approximately temperature-independent strength plateau over a high-temperature interval extending to 1073 K.
A conventional BCC alloy with minimal lattice distortion will consequently be dominated by screw-dislocation plasticity.
The conventional BCC baseline should have lower hardness and more temperature-sensitive flow than the refractory HEAs.

The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase refractory BCC HEAs with significant atomic-size mismatch and may not apply to FCC or multiphase alloys or when precipitation or grain-boundary strengthening dominates.
